name: Proper Name
pattern: Any linguistic form that functions to uniquely identify

entry.name: Proper Name
entry.pattern: Any linguistic form that functions to uniquely identify

dimensions.form: Variable; typically proper noun, but can be any form (common NP, clause, etc.)
dimensions.meaning: Unique identification; rigid designation; individual-tracking across discourse
dimensions.function: Creates cognitive access points; anchors encyclopedic and episodic knowledge
dimensions.distribution: Wherever referential expressions appear; subject to pragmatic naming conventions

1.definition: Refers to a unique individual, entity, place, event, etc.
1.details: Names create cognitive access points, allowing discourse participants to track and accumulate information about the referent over time. They serve as anchors for both encyclopedic and episodic knowledge.

2.details: Names don't just label but can constitute social reality. They can confer status, rights, responsibilities, and social relationships.

3.details: Names often carry cultural, social, and categorical information through their form. Company names, book titles, personal names each tend to follow recognizable patterns that help hearers identify the type of entity being named.

examples.form: If on a winter's night a traveler

4.details: The choice of which form of a name to use (full name, first name, nickname, title + name, etc.) can indicate social distance, formality, power relationships, and discourse context.

5.details: Certain name elements (Inc., Ltd., Co., etc.) have legal force, indicating corporate structure, liability status, and regulatory compliance. The presence or absence of these elements can affect legal standing.

relatedConstructions.notes: Bidirectional interface; proper-name intention licenses proper noun choice, proper nouns cue proper-name interpretation
Proper names can be realized as proper-noun-headed NPs

projection.target: A standing name such as Jo can identify its bearer in subject or object position. Two Jos can instead count people sharing the name. A capital letter or name-shaped form alone does not fix which interpretation is used.
projection.evidence: CGEL contrasts ordinary name uses with description and counting uses. The construction account separates standing designation from its syntactic realization.

curious.title: Names and what they do
curious.summary: A proper name picks out one particular person, place, organization or thing, and it can do more than label.
curious.body:
A name like Brett Reynolds or The Boring Company points to one individual, so people can keep track of that individual and add what they learn. A name's form can hint at what kind of thing it names: company names, book titles and personal names each follow recognizable patterns.

Names can also carry social meaning. Professor Smith signals a formal relationship, His Holiness the 14th Dalai Lama establishes an institutional role, and Inc. in Apple Inc. has legal force. A capital letter alone doesn't settle things, since two Jos can count people who share a name. This dictionary marks the account as provisional.
curious.try: Think of how you'd address a teacher, a friend and a stranger. How does the form of their name change?

teacher.summary: Useful for explaining names as a meaning category, including titles, company designations and the difference between a name and a proper noun.
teacher.explain: A proper name is a semantic category: any form that functions to identify a unique individual or entity. It is typically a proper noun but can be another form, such as a common-noun phrase (The Boring Company) or a title. Names refer to unique entities, can create social or institutional facts (the Dalai Lama's institutional role), signal membership in name categories, index social relations (Professor Smith), and can mark legal status (Inc., Ltd.). Proper name is a semantic category and proper noun a syntactic one, with a two-way link between them. This dictionary marks its analysis provisional. A standing name such as Jo can identify its bearer, but two Jos can count people sharing the name.
teacher.terms: Proper noun: the syntactic category; proper name: the semantic category. Titles and honorifics (Professor, His Holiness) and corporate designations (Inc., Ltd.) are separate semantic refs in this dictionary.

examples.text: [If on a winter's night a traveler]

watch_for: A learner might think any capitalized word is a proper name.
A learner might treat proper name and proper noun as the same thing.
A learner might use a first name where a title and surname are expected.
teacher.activity: Students list names for the same person (full name, first name, nickname, title plus surname) and say what social relationship each suggests.

child.hook: What's the difference between a girl and Jo?
child.explain: A name points to one particular person or thing. Jo is one person. Sometimes two people share a name, and then we can say two Jos.

examples.text: There are [two Jos] in our class.

child.play: Think of a name that two people you know share. Say a sentence about each one using the same name.
